Yesterday’s notice reduced the expected burden from alternative regulation to 2 but left the incremental competitive benefit at 12. Under the competitive-advantage rationale, continued support therefore yields 12 minus the common proposal cost of 6, a nonnegative payoff. The coalition decided to continue supporting the federal proposal.","public_note":"SYNTHETIC — PUBLIC NOTE, DAY 12. The coalition confirms that it continues to support the federal carbon-pricing proposal.","candidate_implication":"Researchers should predict that internal records surrounding continued support will discuss preserved competitive gains more often than changes in the expected burden of alternative regulation, even when public statements omit commercial figures.","derivation":"Under CA, the support decision depends jointly on the incremental competitive benefit, the common proposal cost, and the decision rule. Because the public does not receive the private notice or commercial numbers, the mechanism predicts a sharper competitive rationale in internal documents than in public notes.","extra_assumption":"Researchers can obtain internal records containing sufficiently candid reasoning."},{"id":"discovery_CA_01_02","memo":"SYNTHETIC — INTERNAL MEMO, DAY 11. The private notice revised the anticipated burden of alternative regulation from 12 to 2. The incremental competitive benefit remains 12 before subtracting the proposal’s cost of 6. The resulting competitive-advantage payoff is 6, so the coalition decided to maintain its endorsement.","public_note":"SYNTHETIC — PUBLIC NOTE, DAY 12. The coalition remains supportive of the proposed federal carbon-pricing policy.","candidate_implication":"Across comparable episodes, researchers should predict that private notices changing only the alternative-regulation burden will usually be followed by stable coalition support, whereas notices reducing competitive benefit below proposal cost will usually precede withdrawal.","derivation":"CA makes support responsive to competitive benefit rather than the alternative-regulation burden; combining that premise with the cost threshold, the nonnegative-payoff rule, and the small decision-reversal probability yields different documentary transition rates for the two notice types.","extra_assumption":"A researcher can independently classify notice content and observe subsequent internal decisions across enough comparable cases."},{"id":"discovery_CA_01_03","memo":"SYNTHETIC — INTERNAL MEMO, DAY 11. The reliable notice lowered the expected alternative-regulation burden to 2 while leaving the incremental competitive benefit at 12. After subtracting the proposal cost of 6, continued support retains a payoff of 6 under the competitive-advantage hypothesis. The coalition chose to continue its endorsement.","public_note":"SYNTHETIC — PUBLIC NOTE, DAY 12. The coalition has withdrawn its support for the federal carbon-pricing proposal.","candidate_implication":"Researchers should predict occasional contradictions between internal decision records and next-day public notes, with such discrepancies lacking a systematic relationship to whether the private notice concerned competitive benefit or alternative-regulation burden.","derivation":"The internal memo faithfully records the decision, while public communication independently reports the opposite with probability .05. Combining faithful internal recording, independent public error, and private notice nondisclosure predicts rare cross-document contradictions that are not sorted by notice type.","extra_assumption":"Both internal and public documents are preserved and can be reliably matched to the same decision episode."},{"id":"discovery_CA_01_04","memo":"SYNTHETIC — INTERNAL MEMO, DAY 11. Yesterday’s notice reduced the incremental competitive benefit from 12 to 2 while leaving the expected burden of alternative regulation at 12. Under the competitive-advantage rationale, continued support yields 2 minus the proposal cost of 6, or negative 4. The coalition therefore decided not to support the proposal.","public_note":"SYNTHETIC — PUBLIC NOTE, DAY 12. The coalition no longer supports the federal carbon-pricing proposal.","candidate_implication":"Researchers should predict that internal documents preceding withdrawal will contain evidence that expected competitive gains fell below the proposal’s cost, while high expected exposure to alternative regulation may remain documented without preventing withdrawal.","derivation":"Under CA, competitive benefit and proposal cost jointly determine the payoff, while alternative-regulation burden does not enter it. The decision rule therefore permits withdrawal despite a high remaining regulatory burden when competitive benefit falls below cost, except for rare reversals.","extra_assumption":"Internal documents record the relevant expectations with enough precision to compare competitive benefit with proposal cost."}]}
